source: Gu et al. (2026, ICLR) SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs (v2, adds GPT-5, o1, o3-mini, R1)
finding: Frontier models still show the state-versus-behaviour gap in 2025 versions. Mental-state questions are near ceiling. Behaviour prediction and judgment are much lower. Only o1-preview passes 80% on behaviour. Judgment stays low for all.
quote: Only the o1-preview model, with its built-in inference time reasoning tokens, manages a decent score of more than 80%
limits: Models tested are mid-2024 to Aug 2025; no 2026 frontier model. Two-sentence multiple-choice stories. Humans shown more consistent.
agent_relevance: The gap is not gone in GPT-5 or R1. Our agent should ask for the action only after the state is written down, and check consistency across question types.

source: Gu et al. (2026) SimpleToM, interventions (Table 3, Table 5, Appendix L)
finding: Reminding the model of its own mental-state answer lifts behaviour prediction a lot, but not judgment (except Claude). Plain CoT and a system prompt barely help. The reminder plus a tailored CoT reaches near ceiling, so the gap is about applying, not knowing. No equal-token test was run.
numbers: MS remind, behaviour: GPT-4o 49.5 to 82.8; Llama-3.1-405B 58.3 to 89.5; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 67.0 to 96.9. Judgment with remind: GPT-4o 15.3 to 42.2; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 24.9 to 84.1; Llama-405B ends at 25.8. Generic CoT behaviour: GPT-4o 62.8, judgment 39.2 (Claude 77.2/39.4). Reminder plus tailored CoT: Claude-3.5-Sonnet average 97.1. Tokens: label answer about 2 tokens; CoT* about 230 (GPT-4o), 289 (Claude), 298 (Llama) per behaviour question; o1-preview about 536 reasoning-plus-output tokens.
quote: no simple test-time intervention could reliably patch for the lacking applied ToM capabilities
limits: Three models only; reminder uses the model's own answer to the mental-state question, which costs one extra short call. Cost per question not equalised across arms.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for an 'apply the state to the action' step: it helps at small token cost and beats generic CoT at about 230+ tokens. Gap 1 answered in part; equal-token head-to-head still missing.

source: Saxena, Janzen, Maass (2026) Diagnosing the Explicit-to-Applied Theory of Mind Gap in LLMs (BSTTT)
finding: On three small open models the explicit-to-applied gap on SimpleToM is large and mostly recoverable by a mental-state reminder. Weight updates add only 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond the reminder. Judgment stays below chance. Temporal belief tracking (DynToM) stays hard.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B SimpleToM: overall 51.5%, recognition 99.4%, behaviour 28.9%. Reminder: behaviour 63.2%; reminder+BSTTT 69.7% (+40.8 pts). GPT-oss-20B judgment 3.1% to 18.7% (reminder+BSTTT) or 26.8% (matched ICL). OpenToM: Llama ICL 56.4% vs BSTTT 43.1%. DynToM with annotated state tables: Qwen 42.2, Llama 22.0, GPT-oss 14.5%. Three seeds.
quote: aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance
limits: 7B to 20B models only; multiple choice; authors state the gap may differ in frontier models.
agent_relevance: Independent lab confirms the reminder effect (d02). Supports a cheap 'restate the belief before acting' operator. Providing state tables did not fix dynamic tracking, so a ledger alone is not enough.

source: Nickel, Schrewe, Mai, Flek (2026) Understanding Artificial Theory of Mind: Perturbed Tasks and Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Six open models (Llama 2 70B, Vicuna 33B, Mixtral 8x7B, Yi 34B, Llama 3 70B, DBRX) lose a lot of accuracy under perturbed false-belief tasks, most on transparent-container changes. CoT helps overall but hurts some perturbation classes.
numbers: Dataset 1088 questions, 10 perturbation classes, 7 stages. Average accuracy, vanilla/CoT: unperturbed 67.2/89.6; transparent container 35.4/27.1 (ATE -8.3). Llama 3 70B: unperturbed 100/100, transparent container 25.0/37.5; DBRX: 78.6/100 unperturbed, 62.5/62.5 transparent. Per-class cells are tiny (about 8 items), wide CIs.
quote: steep drop in ToM capabilities under task perturbation for all evaluated LLMs
limits: No frontier or reasoning model (authors excluded them). Table 1 columns garbled in text extraction; per-model cells read with care. Small cells.
agent_relevance: Perturbation drop is concentrated in transparent-access items, as in Ullman. Use as a test set; do not trust CoT as a fix for every class.

source: de Haan, van der Putten, van Duijn (2026a) Reasoning Promotes Robustness in Theory of Mind Tasks
finding: Rewritten Ullman-style modifications run on 2025 reasoning models. Most modifications are solved. Transparent Access (2A) and Relationship Change (2B) still fail for Claude (thinking), Grok-3-mini and R1; GPT-5-high gets half credit on 2A only. Non-thinking Claude is worse on other items.
numbers: Score per item 0, 0.5 or 1; 2 items per variant (14 items). 2A.1/2A.2 and 2B.1/2B.2: Claude, Grok-3-mini, R1 all 0.0; GPT-5-high 2A 0.5/0.5, 2B 0/0. Non-reasoning Claude lost points on 1A, 1B, 1D, 2C (0.5s). Claude thinking vs non-thinking on another test: 100% vs 92%. GPT-5 made one partial mistake across the psychological battery.
quote: Transparent Access and Relationship Change ... are not really trivial
limits: Only 14 items and 5 models, scored by hand; authors say no clear quantification possible. Authors' reading (robustness, not new ToM) is an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 in part: the 2025 drop is concentrated in transparent-access items and shrinks elsewhere. Keep transparent-access items in any regression test.

source: de Haan et al. (2026b, Aug) Evaluating Theory of Mind in Reasoning Models: Robustness over Reasoning (revised version of d05)
finding: Same group, later version of d05. Softens the claim: reasoning gains come at least partly from robustness to prompt and task variation, read as support for a robustness account, not a new ToM skill.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; same experiments as d05. Benchmark-table numbers not used because the extracted table columns were garbled.
limits: Not independent of d05; count once.
agent_relevance: Same as d05.

source: Gong et al. (2026) To Think or Not To Think, That Is The Question for Large Reasoning Models in Theory of Mind Tasks
finding: Nine LLMs on HiToM, ToMATO, ToMBench: reasoning models do not reliably beat non-reasoning siblings. Errors cluster in long responses. More reasoning effort lowers accuracy on higher-order HiToM. A cap near 1,500 tokens helps.
numbers: Qwen3-8B reasoning 0.648 vs non-reasoning 0.705 on ToMATO. GPT-o3 on HiToM: 0.838 at lowest effort to 0.693 at highest. Qwen3-8B-Reasoning capped at 1,500 tokens: 0.706 on HiToM, above both modes. S2F adaptive stop: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B HiToM 0.571 to 0.701 (+22.8%); negligible on first-order ToMBench. Reasoning models keep an edge on ToMBench.
quote: prolonged computation is a liability, not an asset
limits: Interventions only on open models; multiple choice; number of runs per setting not stated.
agent_relevance: Supports a token cap on social-reasoning loops and an adaptive stop; equal-token comparisons matter because more thinking can hurt.

source: Gong et al. (2026), option-removal experiment (same paper as d07)
finding: Removing the multiple-choice options raises reasoning-model accuracy on HiToM but lowers the non-reasoning one. Reasoning models seem to match options instead of deducing. This is an animal-style control condition applied to LLMs.
numbers: HiToM: DeepSeek-R1 0.549 to 0.691 without options; Qwen3-8B-Reasoning 0.481 to 0.629; non-reasoning Qwen3-8B 0.557 to 0.510. Think-to-Match (think without options, then match) helps HiToM but fails on open-ended ToMATO and ToMBench.
limits: HiToM chosen because answers are extractive; effect does not carry to open-ended benchmarks. Same paper as d07; count once.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: control conditions change the ranking of models. Always run a no-options version of each probe.

source: Lu, Zhang, Song, Fan, Wang (2025) Do Theory of Mind Benchmarks Need Explicit Human-like Reasoning in Language Models?
finding: RL on 0.5B to 7B models raises ToM benchmark accuracy, but small models show reasoning collapse (short, meaningless answers with high accuracy). SFT matches or beats RL. Benchmarks can be solved without explicit belief tracking.
numbers: Abstract read: scale-dependent effect (7B good traces, 3B collapse). Per-benchmark numbers not extracted.
limits: Small models; abstract-level numbers.
agent_relevance: Benchmark success is weak evidence of belief tracking. Check traces, not only answers.

source: EnigmaToM (2025) Improve LLMs' Theory-of-Mind Reasoning Capabilities with Neural Knowledge Base of Entity States
finding: Tests an entity-state knowledge base with iterative masking against CoT, SimToM, TimeToM, DWM and PerceptToM on ToMi, HiToM, FANToM. SymbolicToM appears only in a complexity analysis (number of belief graphs), not in the accuracy tables. So no direct SymbolicToM-versus-SimToM accuracy test exists here.
numbers: Seven LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B to GPT-4o). ToMi accuracy, e.g. Gemma2-27B: vanilla 0.767, SimToM 0.749; Enigma variants about 0.79 to 0.87. Gains grow for higher-order ToM up to fourth order. Token counts not equalised.
limits: Table text extraction garbled; exact per-cell numbers uncertain. Complexity argument rests on belief-graph count, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: nobody equalised tokens for ledger versus filter. Structured per-character state still looks best on high-order items.

source: Bawatneh et al. (2026, NeurIPS D&B) OmniToM: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in LLMs via Explicit Belief Modeling
finding: New benchmark scores whether models extract and label the beliefs of every actor, not only the final answer. Built from 895 ToMBench stories with 22,343 belief propositions. It lists SymbolicToM only as a prior benchmark or method; no SymbolicToM-versus-SimToM run.
numbers: 895 stories; 22,343 labeled belief propositions; seven-dimension label schema. Model scores not extracted this session.
limits: Abstract and related work read only.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to test a belief ledger directly (does the ledger match gold beliefs) instead of only final answers.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SAGE: Structured Strategic Reasoning for Efficient LLM Game Playing (independent baseline run of Hypothetical Minds)
finding: An independent team ran Hypothetical Minds as a baseline in three imperfect-information card and dice games. It is among the strongest baselines, best in Goofspiel payoff, but uses huge token counts. The original Melting Pot gain is not tested here.
numbers: Table 1 (mean over 6 opponent types, 30 games per seat): Hypothetical Minds Leduc WR 52.2% payoff +0.817 (vanilla 45.8%, +0.778); Liar's Dice WR 73.6% +0.472 (vanilla 60.8%, +0.217; SAGE 74.7%, +0.494); Goofspiel WR 78.5% +2.836 (vanilla 52.5%, +1.444; SAGE 69.7%, +2.744). Head-to-head SAGE vs Hypothetical Minds: Leduc SAGE WR 30.0% (-1.650), Liar's Dice 50.0%, Goofspiel 61.7%. Liar's Dice tokens: Hypothetical Minds 543,649 per game, 93.5% on history.
limits: Re-implemented by SAGE authors, who propose a rival method. Different domain (games, not Melting Pot). Wins vary by game.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: opponent-hypothesis scaffolds keep a gain over vanilla in an independent test, but token cost is very high and a cheaper structured method matches it.

source: ScrubJay-MEM (2026) Caching for the Future: Scrub Jay Episodic Memory Principles for Agent Memory Systems
finding: Perishability memory was also tested on an external benchmark (MemoryAgentBench EventQA-64k) with a recency baseline. The edge shrinks with a stronger backbone and reverses on conflict-resolution tasks. Same authors for both benchmarks, so still no independent replication.
numbers: EventQA-64k: F1 61.58, EM 41.00 (+2.66 F1 / +5.00 EM over Mem0; +3.09 F1 over Qwen3-Embedding-4B). Stronger backbone qwen3:30b: Contriever F1 78.68 vs ScrubJay-MEM 72.82. TGT (20 instances, 1,320 queries, single seed 42): GenGap +0.108 full; flat recency baseline B5 -0.046; dense top-1 -0.022; no-decay +0.019 (5.7x drop); LLM-only +0.181 at 44.4% accuracy (artifact). MAB ConflictResolution: mechanism actively miscalibrated.
limits: Single seed, benchmark built by the authors with LLM naturalisation; baselines weaker than a tuned production memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Perishability helps small backbones on temporal questions; do not add it as a default rule. Test per task type.

source: Dally, Emery, Clayton (2006) Food-caching western scrub-jays keep track of who was watching when (Science 312:1662); Clayton et al. (2007) review abstract
finding: Abstract only. Jays remember which individual watched which caching event and re-cache accordingly. The paper found NO evidence that cache protection is cued by the observer's behaviour. So Dally 2006 is not a deception study; the earlier critique used the wrong label. Its null on cues is consistent with Amodio 2021.
numbers: Abstract has no numbers; full text not accessible (not open access).
quote: We found no evidence to suggest that a storer's use of cache protection tactics is cued by the observer's behavior.
limits: Abstract only. Same Cambridge lab and mostly the same birds as the later work.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 correction: 'who watched when' is memory of a source, which maps to tracking who holds which fact, not to mind-reading.

source: Vernouillet, Huang, Kelly (2025) Pinyon jays and Clark's nutcrackers can discriminate between pilfering and non-pilfering conspecifics, but not heterospecifics (Anim Cogn 28:19)
finding: An independent lab (Manitoba) with two other corvid species finds cachers re-cache more from the tray given to a pilfering conspecific than a non-pilfering one, but not for heterospecific observers. Birds also re-cached more after caching near a conspecific than alone. This is learned pilferer identity, not desire-state or perspective reading.
numbers: 6 pinyon jays and 5 Clark's nutcrackers as cachers; conditions Alone, Objects, Conspecifics, Heterospecifics; 3 blocks; re-caching fell over blocks; females re-cached more; conspecific vs alone effect reported as a large z value (exact value cut in extraction).
limits: Small n. Does not test Ostojic 2017 (desire-state) or Legg and Clayton 2014 (observer perspective).
agent_relevance: Independent-lab support for 'track who is a risk and re-check exposed items'; says nothing about perspective-taking. Gap 4 stays open for the desire-state claim.

source: Kano, Krupenye, Hirata, Tomonaga, Call (2019) Great apes use self-experience to anticipate an agent's action in a false-belief test (PNAS)
finding: Eye-tracked apes watched a video of an actor behind a barrier the ape had felt as translucent or opaque. Only apes who experienced the barrier as opaque anticipated the actor's mistaken search. This goes against the behaviour-rule account, because the video was identical.
numbers: Between-subjects design; abstract has no counts (full text not opened).
limits: Abstract only; small ape samples; same research network as Krupenye 2016, so not an independent lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly: the best follow-up to Krupenye 2016 adds an experience-based control. Same logic as an agent test where the cue stays fixed but the hidden fact changes.

source: Kampis et al. (2021) A two-lab direct replication attempt of Southgate, Senju and Csibra (2007)
finding: The anticipatory-looking false-belief paradigm that Krupenye 2016 adapted for apes failed a close direct replication in infants. About half of infants looked at the agent's action location, with or without a false belief.
numbers: 160 infants aged 25 months across two sites. Original: 20 infants, 10 per condition. In a follow-up analysis 49 infants gave the correct first look and 41 did not. No evidence for action anticipation or belief-based anticipation.
quote: we were unable to replicate the original finding of Southgate et al.
limits: Infants, not apes. Authors cite several other non-replications and say the paradigm may not suit this question.
agent_relevance: The method behind the ape result is fragile. No pre-registered large replication in apes was found (gap 6 remains open).

source: Tauzin (2025) Communicative mentalization is limited in nonhuman great apes (PNAS letter, on Townrow and Krupenye)
finding: Argues that bonobos pointing more for an ignorant than a knowledgeable human can come from learned reward rules, because familiarization and test trials matched. Says novel tasks with bigger samples show apes modify points but do not tailor them to ignorance, unlike human infants.
numbers: No new data; argument that apes were rewarded in about one third of unpointed ignorance trials.
limits: Letter; a reply exists (Reply to Tauzin) that was not read.
agent_relevance: Same low-level alternative lens as K09: ask whether the agent's social move could come from a learned rule.

source: Krupenye and Call (2019) Theory of mind in animals: current and future directions (WIREs Cogn Sci)
finding: Review abstract: some species share foundational social-cognitive mechanisms with humans; new work adds belief and desire attribution tests, critical controls, and new species (lemurs, dogs).
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only; the review authors ran the 2016 study.
agent_relevance: Background.

source: Kulke, Reiss, Krist, Rakoczy (2018) Implicit false belief across the lifespan: non-replication of an anticipatory looking task (Cognitive Development)
finding: Title and citation count only (43). Reported non-replication of an anticipatory-looking false-belief task across ages.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Pointer.

source: Development of cognition in corvids (2026, Anim Cogn), systematic review of 47 studies over 16 species
finding: Abstract via Europe PMC search: structured review of corvid cognitive development 2005 onward, with discussion of methodological robustness. Full text fetch timed out.
numbers: 47 studies, 16 species.
limits: Abstract level; about development, not adult replications.
agent_relevance: No independent raven replication was found in searches (gap 5 stays open).
